**United States Postal Service — the handwriting nobody could write a rule for (1997-2011)**

Printed addresses were readable by software decades ago: the shapes are consistent, so a program can be told what each character looks like. Handwriting defeated that approach. Every writer forms a 7 differently. No rule you can write down covers a nation posting its Christmas cards.

So the Postal Service did not write one. With researchers at the State University of New York at Buffalo and Lockheed Martin, it deployed a learning-based address reader before the 1997 Christmas season. It was shown enormous numbers of scanned envelopes each paired with its correct address, and worked out the patterns itself. That learning happened once, offline; what runs on the sorting line is the finished reader, deciding fast on envelopes it has never seen.

It did not arrive finished. Buffalo puts the first version below 2 per cent on handwritten mail; Government Executive reported in February 1999 that it read handwritten addresses correctly 30 to 40 per cent of the time and had saved at least $90 million in its first year; Buffalo cites about 93 per cent of hand-lettered envelopes by 2011. It never reached certainty: what the machines cannot read confidently is photographed and sent to human operators at a remote encoding centre, as Smithsonian reported in 2016.

Carry that shape into the AI products you manage. Nobody specified the behaviour; examples did. The error rate fell over years rather than being closed by a release. What made the system usable was not a cleverer model but an honest admission that some answers would be wrong, and a human path for the ones it was unsure about.

**Instacart — a model still right about a world that had stopped existing (2020)**

Every Instacart order is picked by a person walking a real supermarket, so the app has to guess whether each item is actually on the shelf. Promising something that is not there wrecks the order. A model trained on historical shopper data made that call.

Then, in mid-March 2020, shoppers emptied the shelves. Fortune reported that the accuracy of the measure Instacart used to judge item-availability predictions fell from 93 per cent to 61 per cent. No code shipped and no model changed. Customers were buying flour, hand sanitiser and toilet paper in quantities the training data had never contained, and stock ran out at hours it never had. Instacart's own engineering account describes a near-30 per cent drop in ordered items being found early that month.

The repair was to the data, not the algorithm. Instacart's machine learning director Sharath Rao told Fortune the disruption was "a shock to the system" and that "every day looks like a Monday for Instacart". The team retrained on only the previous ten days instead of several weeks — trading volume for freshness — and rescored items hourly rather than every three hours. Accuracy came back to about 85 per cent, still below where it had started.

This is what the lifecycle loop is for. A held-out test set gives an honest estimate of performance on data drawn from the world the training data came from; it cannot warn you that the world is about to move. Deployment is a stage, not an ending — and deciding which number you watch, how often, and what decay triggers a retrain is a product decision made before launch, not during the emergency.

**Epic Systems — the sepsis alert that fired 6,971 times and was right 843 times (2018-2021)**

Sepsis kills quickly, so hospitals want early warning. Epic, whose electronic health record runs a large share of US hospitals, shipped a sepsis prediction model that scored every admitted patient and alerted above a set score. Epic's documentation reported an AUC of 0.76 to 0.83 — one number summarising how well a model separates sick from well across every possible cut-off. Hundreds of hospitals switched it on.

In June 2021 a Michigan Medicine team published an independent check in JAMA Internal Medicine: 38,455 hospitalisations, 2,552 involving sepsis. Their AUC came out at 0.63. More telling was the model at the threshold hospitals actually ran, a score of six or above. Recall was 33 per cent — it missed 1,709 of the 2,552 sepsis cases. Precision was 12 per cent — it alerted on 6,971 hospitalisations, 18 per cent of everyone admitted, and about seven in eight of those alerts concerned a patient without sepsis.

Both errors at once. Low precision meant a false alarm most times the tool spoke, which is how alert fatigue begins. Low recall meant the alerts staff did heed were missing two-thirds of what the system existed to catch.

Nothing was concealed by dishonesty. It was concealed by the choice of metric: AUC averages across thresholds nobody deploys, while precision and recall describe the product as it behaves on the ward. When anyone hands you a single summary figure, ask this lesson's questions instead. At the threshold we will really run, how often is a flag correct, how many real cases do we catch, and which error costs more?

**Presto Automation — the drive-thru voice AI whose cost per order never fell (2021-2025)**

Presto Automation sold Presto Voice to American fast-food chains including Carl's Jr., Del Taco and Checkers. The pitch was pure unit economics: let the AI take the drive-thru order and the restaurant stops paying someone to take it. Presto publicly claimed 95 per cent of orders were handled without human intervention.

The company's own filings with the US Securities and Exchange Commission told a different story. Presto disclosed that more than 70 per cent of orders running through its in-house Presto Voice needed a human agent — off-site staff in countries including the Philippines and India — to complete them. Later filings reported that at pilot sites running its most advanced version, about 30 per cent of orders needed no human to enter them, rising to 46 per cent a quarter on. In January 2025 the SEC settled charges that Presto had made materially false and misleading statements about the product.

Read past the enforcement and the economics are stark. A restaurant was being sold the removal of a per-order labour cost, and that cost had not been removed. Every order still carried a human, plus the compute, plus the platform. Cost per use sat above the value the product was priced on, and no volume would fix it, because the cost scaled with the orders.

That is this lesson's trap, plainly. Before committing to an AI feature, work out what one use genuinely costs — inference, retries, fallbacks, and any human who checks or rescues the output — and compare it with what one use is worth. A feature that loses money per call loses more the more successful it becomes.

**Rite Aid — a surveillance system nobody was told about and nobody tested (2012-2023)**

From at least October 2012 to July 2020, the US pharmacy chain Rite Aid ran facial recognition in hundreds of stores, matching shoppers against an internal list of suspected shoplifters. Staff were told not to mention it to customers or the press.

In December 2023 the Federal Trade Commission set out the consequences: thousands of false matches. Customers were tailed, refused service, searched and reported to police on the strength of a wrong match; one employee stopped and searched an 11-year-old girl the system had flagged. Rite Aid, the FTC alleged, never tested the technology's accuracy before or after switching it on, never tracked its false-positive rate, enrolled people from low-quality images that made false matches likelier, and did not train the staff acting on its output.

The burden fell unevenly. About 80 per cent of Rite Aid's stores sat in plurality-White areas, yet the complaint alleged the technology was concentrated in stores whose customers were mostly Black, Asian and Latino. The order barred Rite Aid from facial-recognition surveillance for five years and made it delete the biometric data gathered.

Notice how little of this concerns the model. Rite Aid was not undone by a weak algorithm but by the absence of everything around it: no accuracy measurement, no comparison of outcomes across groups, no notice to those being scored, no training for staff acting on its verdicts, and no route for someone wrongly accused to challenge it. Those are this lesson's governance duties, and they belong to whoever ships the product, not the vendor who supplied the model.
